question: Can permutation symmetry and small initialization reduce many smooth neural architectures to one quadratic order-parameter dynamics that explains both abrupt, mode-wise learning events and smooth power-law loss decay over training time?

key_findings.claim: For a smooth module built as a sum over exchangeable components, permutation symmetry plus zero gradient when one component is zero forces the leading nonconstant small-weight expansion to depend on the component weights only through the quadratic moment M=WW-transpose.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 gives f_x(W)=f_x(0)+Tr[WW^T A(x)]+O(||W||^3), with an O(||W||^4) remainder under per-component sign symmetry. Without the zero-gradient condition, the appendix adds first-moment terms but retains closure on M and mu.

key_findings.claim: MLPs, CNNs, attention, and mixture-of-experts modules share the same quadratic form but differ through a computable structure matrix A(x); for ordinary multi-head attention near zero, value and readout blocks appear at quadratic order while query and key enter only at quartic order.
key_findings.evidence: Propositions 1 through 6 derive explicit block matrices for two-layer MLPs, single-layer CNNs, full and query-key-only attention, and independently gated experts. The full-attention A matrix has nonzero value-readout blocks determined by the mean context token, whereas query-key interaction appears in a different quadratic model only when value and readout are fixed.

key_findings.claim: NQF training under SGD closes exactly on two low-order statistics, and, on the finite training set, width beyond the joint data subspace is dynamically redundant after a specific rescaling.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 writes discrete updates for mu=sum_i w_i and M=sum_i w_i w_i^T without tracking individual neurons. Theorem 3 states that an NQF wider than k_V+1 can be replaced by one of width k_V+1 while preserving predictions at every SGD step on the training set, provided A and the learning rate are rescaled inversely with width.

key_findings.claim: When the sample structure matrices commute, gradient flow becomes a generalized Lotka-Volterra system over nonnegative feature eigenvalues, and several restricted data geometries admit exact solutions.
key_findings.evidence: A shared eigenbasis reduces prediction and loss to diagonal features z_k. Their dynamics contain growth terms from target alignment and pairwise competition or cooperation from sample correlations. Theorems 4 through 7 solve proportional samples, orthogonal samples, orthogonal features, and an isotropic noncommuting case.

key_findings.claim: Small initialization separates feature ignition times logarithmically, while a power-law distribution of mode growth rates and target strengths merges many sharp events into a predictable training-time power law.
key_findings.evidence: For effective mode growth rate zeta_k, ignition occurs at t*_k proportional to zeta_k^{-1} log(1/epsilon), so gaps diverge as epsilon approaches zero. If zeta_k scales as k^{-alpha_2} and target strength V_k as k^{-alpha_1}, excess loss scales as training time to -(alpha_1-1)/alpha_2; an analogous sample-wise theorem gives exponent -(2 gamma_1-1)/gamma_2.

key_findings.claim: Experiments support the local approximation at small initialization and the predicted solvable dynamics, but also expose the approximation's finite neighborhood.
key_findings.evidence: Across synthetic MLP, CNN, query-key attention, and multi-head attention experiments with gradient descent, momentum, and Adam, the NQF follows the original at initialization scale 0.01 and diverges visibly at 0.2. In teacher-student MLP and attention runs it tracks for roughly the first 100 of 2,000 steps before separating; on a 4,000-example MNIST odd-versus-even task, one-layer NQFs and the corresponding models show similar training and test trajectories. Synthetic feature- and sample-wise experiments recover predicted plateaus and Fourier-MLP power-law slopes.

method.core_idea: Apply a Landau-style symmetry expansion around small initialization, compute one architecture-specific quadratic coefficient matrix, and study training through the invariant second moment instead of individual parameters.
method.mechanism: A width-d module is partitioned into exchangeable parameter blocks w_i. Smoothness and component permutation symmetry constrain its Taylor series; under the zero-gradient-at-zero condition, linear and cross-component quadratic terms vanish, leaving a sum of w_i^T A(x) w_i. Loss gradients therefore factor through M=WW^T (and through mu when the condition is removed), yielding closed SGD or gradient-flow equations. With commuting A(x_mu), simultaneous diagonalization turns M's eigenvalues into interacting feature abundances governed by a generalized Lotka-Volterra equation. Logistic-like feature growth from tiny initial mass creates delayed ignition; a heavy-tailed spectrum of ignition rates and target energies converts the staircase into an aggregate power law.
assumptions: Each analyzed module can be partitioned into genuinely exchangeable minimal components under a permutation symmetry.
The module is at least three-times continuously differentiable near the zero parameter configuration.
Initialization remains small relative to data-dependent feature scales for long enough that discarded cubic and higher terms are negligible.
The simplified theorem assumes each component's gradient vanishes when that component is zero; the more general form adds first-moment couplings.
Exact Lotka-Volterra reductions require commuting structure matrices or a special isotropic second-moment condition.
The training-time scaling theorem assumes, rather than derives, power-law mode growth rates and target strengths.
Most exact solutions use squared error and gradient flow, although the moment closure itself covers discrete SGD and some linear-update optimizers.

techniques.role: Uses exchangeability to eliminate most Taylor coefficients and isolate the lowest symmetry-allowed collective interaction.
Encodes the input-dependent sparsity and couplings of each module in A(x), enabling comparisons before training.
Tracks M=WW^T and optionally mu=sum_i w_i so dynamics do not scale with the number of exchangeable units.
Constructs a narrower NQF whose rescaled structure and learning rate reproduce training-set predictions at every SGD step.
Diagonalizes commuting sample matrices and discards off-diagonal moment coordinates that do not affect predictions.
Interprets modes as species with target-driven growth and correlation-driven competition or cooperation, exposing solvable regimes.
Rescales time by log(1/epsilon) so smooth logistic growth converges to separated saddle-to-saddle feature activations.
Integrates power-law-distributed feature or sample ignition events to derive macroscopic loss exponents.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic low-rank NQF teacher with 600 samples and four student architectures: two-layer tanh MLP, one-layer CNN, query-key-only attention, and four-head attention; gradient descent, Polyak momentum 0.9, and Adam.
evaluations.metric: Recovered teacher singular modes over training for original module versus its NQF expansion.
evaluations.result: At Gaussian initialization scale sigma=0.01, NQF and original trajectories nearly coincide across the displayed optimizers and architectures; at sigma=0.2 they visibly separate.
evaluations.baseline: The unapproximated architecture initialized with the same weights.

evaluations.setting: Online teacher-student regression for a 100-hidden-unit tanh MLP and four-head query-key attention over 2,000 SGD steps from epsilon=0.001.
evaluations.metric: Agreement of original and NQF learning trajectories.
evaluations.result: Both approximations track their original models for roughly 100 steps and then diverge, directly delimiting the local approximation window.

evaluations.setting: MNIST odd-versus-even classification with 4,000 examples, MSE loss, full-batch Adam, epsilon=0.01; two-layer MLP, one-layer CNN, and one-layer attention.
evaluations.metric: Training loss and test accuracy trajectories.
evaluations.result: The paper reports similar or visually indistinguishable trajectories between each architecture and its NQF counterpart; no scalar approximation error, confidence interval, or seed variation is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Original MLP, CNN, or attention model.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic orthogonal-feature system with five modes and epsilon=1e-5, plus a 1,000-mode constructed power-law system.
evaluations.metric: Mode eigenvalue trajectories, plateau transition times, and excess-loss log-log slope.
evaluations.result: Gradient-descent markers follow the analytic logistic curves; sharp loss drops align with predicted half-saturation times; the aggregate slope matches the asymptotic exponent up to the derived finite-initialization steepening.
evaluations.baseline: Closed-form Theorem 6 dynamics and predicted scaling exponent.

evaluations.setting: Four mutually orthogonal synthetic samples with block-diagonal structure matrices.
evaluations.metric: Per-sample residual and total-MSE transition timing.
evaluations.result: Full-batch gradient descent follows the numerically integrated Theorem 5 trajectory and learns samples in separated steps.
evaluations.baseline: Runge-Kutta solution of the reduced auxiliary ODE.

evaluations.setting: Fourier-feature tanh MLP with 64 modes and 256 grid points, power-law feature scales and targets, epsilon=1e-4.
evaluations.metric: Normalized MSE as a function of training time and fitted power-law exponent across theta values.
evaluations.result: The Fourier MLP and its NQF follow the predicted t^{-(2 beta-1)/(theta+beta)} behavior, while a standard tanh MLP on the raw scalar input does not show the same law.
evaluations.baseline: NQF approximation, analytic exponent, and an ordinary raw-input MLP.

limitations: Author-stated: the NQF is a local expansion and fails when initialization or subsequent parameter motion is large relative to the feature scale.
Author-stated: ReLU at the origin, biases, normalization layers, and nonlinearities applied after component aggregation violate the main theorem's smoothness or structural assumptions.
Author-stated: cubic and higher-order terms create additional plateaus not captured by the quadratic theory; multilayer treatment is only preliminary.
Author-stated: power-law spectra are assumptions of the scaling result, not consequences of architecture or realistic data.
Author-stated: the optimizer closure covers gradient descent, weight decay, and Polyak momentum but not Adam, despite empirical tracking in tested cases.

Reviewer inference: the order-parameter dimension is independent of width d but scales with p, the parameter count of one exchangeable component; for an attention head p can itself be large, so this is not automatically a practical compression.

Reviewer inference: the exact dynamics mostly concern squared loss and highly structured synthetic data, while real language-model training uses cross-entropy, normalization, residual composition, adaptive optimization, and non-small trajectories.
Reviewer inference: the main real-data evidence is a small MNIST binary task without repeated seeds or quantitative approximation-error summaries.
failure_modes: At finite or large initialization, higher-order terms can rotate or couple modes before the quadratic ignition times and destroy the predicted staircase.
Layer normalization, biases, residual interactions, and post-aggregation nonlinearities can introduce lower- or same-order terms not represented by the proposed A matrix.
Noncommuting sample matrices prevent simultaneous diagonalization, so off-diagonal moment dynamics can feed predictions and the ecological mode interpretation may fail.
Power-law loss will not emerge if mode rates or target strengths lack a sufficiently broad power-law range; finite rank then produces crossovers or plateaus instead.
A mode with nonpositive effective growth rate never ignites, and weight decay shifts the stability threshold rather than merely delaying learning.
Training-set dynamical equivalence need not imply equal predictions off the training support or equal generalization after compression.
First-order agreement under Adam in small experiments may be accidental because coordinate-wise preconditioning depends on parameter-level statistics not closed by M and mu.
reusable_insights: Before simulating a wide module, derive the lowest symmetry-allowed expansion and identify which parameter blocks can matter at each order.
Use invariant moments to separate genuine collective dynamics from redundant permutations of exchangeable units.
Treat sudden-learning steps and smooth scaling curves as different resolutions of the same event-time distribution.
Measure initialization dependence explicitly: a log(1/epsilon) shift is diagnostic of multiplicative feature growth from a near-zero unstable state.
Check whether sample or feature operators approximately commute; near-joint diagonalizability can suggest a useful reduced model even when exact solvability fails.
Distinguish training-time scaling from model-, data-, and compute-scaling laws before comparing exponents.
Report where a local surrogate stops tracking, not only the interval in which it succeeds.
open_questions: Can a controlled expansion including normalization, bias, residual streams, and nonsmooth activations yield a useful normal form for modern transformers?
Do empirically measured structure-matrix spectra in realistic language or vision data exhibit the assumed power-law tails over enough decades to predict loss exponents?
Can the moment dynamics predict held-out generalization, grokking, or transfer rather than only optimization loss?
How does approximate noncommutativity perturb ignition order and the Lotka-Volterra interpretation?
Is there a parameter-level closure for Adam or other adaptive preconditioners that preserves the NQF reduction?
Can higher-order neural cubic or quartic forms explain the plateaus the quadratic model misses without losing tractability?
Does the width-compressed dynamically equivalent NQF generalize like the original network on unseen inputs?

competitive_landscape.title: Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Saxe, McClelland, and Ganguli derive exact mode-wise plateaus and rapid transitions for deep linear networks under special data and initialization conditions; NQF derives a shared quadratic local form for several nonlinear module families and connects the same logistic mode dynamics to aggregate power laws.

competitive_landscape.title: SGD learning on neural networks: leap complexity and saddle-to-saddle dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbe, Boix-Adsera, and Misiakiewicz prove sequential support learning and SGD complexity for low-dimensional targets under isotropic data and two-layer networks; NQF instead obtains saddle-to-saddle behavior from multiplicative order-parameter growth and emphasizes architecture unification and loss scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: A Solvable Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Maloney, Roberts, and Sully solve a random-feature statistical model for test-loss scaling with dataset and parameter size; NQF studies excess training loss over time in a feature-learning dynamics and explicitly separates that target from resource-scaling laws.

competitive_landscape.title: How Feature Learning Can Improve Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon, Atanasov, and Pehlevan give a solvable beyond-kernel model where feature learning changes training-time and compute exponents by task difficulty; NQF derives the feature dynamics from permutation symmetry and ties individual mode ignition to the aggregate exponent.

competitive_landscape.title: Quadratic models for understanding catapult dynamics of neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhu et al. use a neural quadratic model to reproduce large-learning-rate catapult dynamics and generalization behavior; this paper derives rather than posits its quadratic form for exchangeable modules and focuses on small-initialization feature ignition instead of large-step instability.

competitive_landscape.title: A Defense of the Quadratic Model
competitive_landscape.difference: Meterez et al. Taylor-expand the full optimization problem at intermediate LLM checkpoints and empirically predict windows up to roughly ten percent of training while analyzing Hessian structure and stability; NQF expands each exchangeable module near zero, keeps feature-learning nonlinearity through M, and supplies exact mode dynamics under structured data.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Permutation symmetry turns many architectures and seventeen previously separate solvable proxies into one neural quadratic form whose order-parameter dynamics jointly explain sudden learning and training-time scaling laws.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Quadratic surrogates, deep-linear plateaus, saddle-to-saddle learning, and spectral scaling theories all predate the paper. The new technical combination is the symmetry-derived architecture matrix, exact moment closure and training-set compression, Lotka-Volterra reduction, and one event-based account linking plateaus to power-law loss.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The normal-form and unification result appears genuinely distinctive within its assumptions. The broad deep-learning universality claim is not yet established: modern-network violations are central rather than peripheral, and most scaling evidence is constructed synthetic data plus a small MNIST check.

reviewer_notes: The complete 52-page extraction was checked, including theorem statements, proof appendices, removal of the ZGZ condition, optimizer and multilayer extensions, compression error, NTK discussion, and experimental details. Formula descriptions are paraphrased in plain text but retain the paper's exponents and limit order. Competitive metadata and methodological distinctions were checked against primary arXiv records.
